title: Augustine's Confessions
hookLine: a book about a life, written the whole way through as a prayer to God

cards: A teenager and his friends climb into a neighbor's orchard at night and strip a pear tree. They aren't hungry; they have better pears at home. They take a bite or two and throw the rest to the pigs.

You met those pears back in year three. Years later, the thief is a bishop named Augustine, and he can't stop asking why he did it. His uncomfortable answer: because it was forbidden, and because his friends were there.
The story sits in a book called the Confessions, and here's the strange part. It isn't written to us. Page after page, it's written to God.

teach.b: The Confessions open with praise, borrowing a psalm: great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. Then comes the sentence that holds the whole book.

In Pusey's old translation, Augustine says to God: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." That's the map. The rest is Augustine telling how restless he was.
He chased learning, success, and applause as a teacher of speech. He chased love, and loved badly. He tried one philosophy after another.
Each, he says, was a place he hoped to rest, and none of them held.
The word confession does two jobs here. It means owning up: the pears, the pride, the people he hurt. And it means praise: confessing who God is.
Augustine does both in the same breath, so the book reads like one long conversation, him talking and listening for an answer. The turn comes in a garden in Milan.
He's weeping under a fig tree, sick of himself, when he hears a child's voice from a nearby house, chanting: "Take up and read; Take up and read."
He opens the letters of Paul where they fall, and reads: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh." He says the shadows of doubt fled away.

Christians in different churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, still read the Confessions. Some come for the conversion. Some come for the honesty: a bishop, writing down that he stole fruit to impress his friends.

how: Christians of different churches read Augustine's Confessions as a spiritual classic, and some keep a prayer journal in the same spirit, writing to God directly about their lives.

games.q: you're Augustine, weeping under a fig tree. a child's voice keeps chanting, take up and read. what do you do?
o: go find the child and ask what the game is.
open the book of Paul's letters and read where it falls.
leave the garden and go to bed.
games.why: he picks up Paul's letters and reads the first passage his eyes fall on. he says the shadows of doubt fled away.

practice: Write one short paragraph to God, the way Augustine does, or, if you don't pray, a letter you're not sure where to send. Say one true thing about where you are today: what you're chasing, what you're tired of, what you're glad of.
Don't polish it; Augustine didn't hide the pears.

wordCard.voice: Augustine's Confessions. The story of a restless life, told as a prayer: owning up to what he did, and praising the God he says he was looking for all along.

orig.note: Latin: confessions. Augustine's title carries both senses, owning up and praising God.

carryVoice: Your line: our heart is restless. Augustine's whole book hangs on it. Rest well.
